nodes.title: The Kissinger Doctrine
nodes.description: American power must serve a political settlement. Selective pressure, diplomatic openings and limited commitments can divide rival coalitions without requiring another unlimited war.

nodes.title: Limited Commitments
nodes.description: A small number of closely supervised commitments protects sensitive channels and concentrates American resources.

nodes.title: Expanded Mandates
nodes.description: A broader programme lets Washington challenge several opponents at once, at the cost of greater administrative demands and political exposure.

nodes.title: Triangular Diplomacy
nodes.description: The divisions between Moscow and Beijing offer room for negotiation and strategic leverage.
requirements: Either mandate policy

nodes.title: Deniable Pressure
nodes.description: Financial support, political contacts and limited material aid can burden a hostile government. Local partners retain their own interests and demands.
requirements: Either mandate policy

nodes.title: Regional Guarantees
nodes.description: Diplomatic commitments and limited security assistance give regional partners an alternative to escalation.
requirements: Either mandate policy

nodes.title: A Channel to Beijing
nodes.description: A confidential channel can serve both Washington and Beijing without settling every dispute between them.
requirements: China accepts the proposed terms

nodes.title: Détente with Moscow
nodes.description: Arms-control talks and regular high-level contact offer a channel through which competition can be contained.
requirements: Soviet acceptance

nodes.title: Contest Soviet Clients
nodes.description: Opposition to a Soviet-aligned government must rest on a viable local partner and a sustained political objective.

nodes.title: The Angolan Front
nodes.description: Aid to Angolan movements can contest Soviet and Cuban influence, while domestic opposition and the conduct of local partners constrain American commitments.
requirements: Angolan independence or a genuine civil-war crisis
An eligible local movement accepts aid

nodes.title: Political Operations
nodes.description: Media, political organisations and sympathetic institutions can contest an opponent through sustained political competition.

nodes.title: The Chilean Opposition
nodes.description: Support for opposition parties and media can challenge a hostile government. Chilean political actors decide whether to cooperate and how to act.
requirements: A hostile political confrontation in Chile
A local organisation accepts cooperation

nodes.title: Shuttle Diplomacy
nodes.description: Repeated negotiations can turn limited military outcomes into a durable regional settlement.
requirements: The affected governments accept each agreement

nodes.title: The Kurdish Question
nodes.description: The Kurdish populations of Iraq, Iran, Turkey and Syria live under different governments and political movements. American policy must choose its commitments country by country.

nodes.title: Open Barzani Channels
nodes.description: Contacts with Barzani offer a route into northern Iraq. Political cooperation must precede any commitment of American money or equipment.
requirements: A willing Iraqi Kurdish political partner

nodes.title: The Iranian Connection
nodes.description: Iran can provide the transit and liaison essential to a sustained assistance programme. Tehran must agree to the arrangement.
requirements: Iran accepts transit and liaison access

nodes.title: An Anatolian Channel
nodes.description: A separate agreement with Ankara can sustain access to northern Iraq if the Iranian channel is unavailable. Turkey decides whether to accept the arrangement.
requirements: Turkey accepts transit and liaison access

nodes.title: Sustain the Peshmerga
nodes.description: A limited flow of money and material can preserve Kurdish bargaining power and tie down Iraqi forces. It creates a commitment that Washington must be prepared to sustain.
requirements: Either active, accepted delivery channel
A consenting local partner
Strategic confrontation with Baghdad
One available campaign slot

nodes.title: Bargain for Autonomy
nodes.description: Use American leverage to secure regional rights within Iraq. A negotiated agreement can preserve Kurdish institutions while ending the armed confrontation.

nodes.title: Arm the Mountain Front
nodes.description: Escalate assistance to an armed opposition. Baghdad receives time to reinforce the region or offer a political settlement before an uprising becomes possible.

nodes.title: Guarantee the Settlement
nodes.description: A settlement requires Baghdad and the Kurdish representatives to accept its terms. Its guarantees remain conditional on the agreement being respected.
requirements: Iraq and Kurdish representatives accept regional autonomy

nodes.title: Back a Separate Kurdistan
nodes.description: Independence is a separate political objective with a greater regional cost. Recognition follows actual Kurdish control and a decision by Kurdish representatives.
requirements: A successful local uprising
Actual Kurdish control of eligible territory
Kurdish representatives seek independence

nodes.title: The Iranian Dossier
nodes.description: The Shah is an American partner in the 1970 opening. A Kurdish pressure programme against Tehran requires a genuine confrontation or a deliberate break with that partnership.
requirements: Hostile Iranian government or a deliberate breach with Tehran

nodes.title: Zagros Political Networks
nodes.description: Iranian Kurdish representatives have their own programmes and loyalties. They must consent to assistance independently of any Iraqi movement.
requirements: A willing Iranian Kurdish political partner

nodes.title: Fund the Mountain Committees
nodes.description: Sustained support can strengthen local organisation. The Iranian government can answer with regional investment, security deployments or negotiations.
requirements: Accepted transit or another paid delivery route
One available campaign slot

nodes.title: A Federal Bargain
nodes.description: Seek local rights through an accepted constitutional settlement rather than a separation imposed from abroad.

nodes.title: Challenge Tehran in the North
nodes.description: An armed programme raises the price of confrontation for Tehran and exposes Washington to a wider regional dispute.

nodes.title: Recognise a Kurdish Claim
nodes.description: Recognition depends on an actual local political authority and territory it can hold. It does not transfer another Kurdish government or its population to American control.
requirements: A successful local uprising
Kurdish local authority controls the eligible region
A local request for independence

nodes.title: The Turkish Dossier
nodes.description: Turkey is a NATO ally in the 1970 opening. Cooperation and confrontation are distinct policies with consequences for the wider alliance.

nodes.title: Preserve the Alliance
nodes.description: Offer Ankara an intelligence partnership and support a negotiated regional approach. The agreement must be accepted by Turkey.
requirements: Actual shared NATO membership
Turkish acceptance

nodes.title: Challenge an Ally
nodes.description: A deliberate confrontation with Ankara sacrifices alliance trust for freedom of action. Regional opposition will not become an American instrument merely because Washington offers aid.
requirements: A deliberate breach of cooperation, or an existing strategic confrontation

nodes.title: Contacts in the Southeast
nodes.description: Approach local Kurdish political representatives. Their demands and political loyalties will shape the terms of any American assistance.
requirements: A willing Turkish Kurdish political partner
One available campaign slot

nodes.title: Regional Rights Negotiations
nodes.description: A political agreement can reduce the conflict while preserving Turkey as a single state. Both Ankara and the local representatives determine its terms.
requirements: Active alliance cooperation or a consenting regional political network

nodes.title: Support an Armed Alternative
nodes.description: Military support is a major escalation against Ankara. Success depends on local organisation and on the response of the Turkish government.

nodes.title: Endorse a Separate State
nodes.description: A separate state is a possible alternative outcome of a successful local struggle, rather than an automatic result of American sponsorship.
requirements: A successful local uprising
Kurdish local authority controls the eligible region
A local independence request

nodes.title: Syrian Kurdish Contacts
nodes.description: Approach Kurdish political representatives in northern Syria. Their regional demands remain distinct from those of movements in neighbouring states.

nodes.title: A Voice in the North
nodes.description: Political and civic support can strengthen local representation without beginning an armed confrontation.
requirements: A willing local organisation
One available campaign slot

nodes.title: Regional Organisation
nodes.description: Build a political network capable of negotiating with Damascus or sustaining a longer confrontation.

nodes.title: Citizenship and Local Rights
nodes.description: A negotiated framework can address citizenship and local administration while preserving the Syrian state.

nodes.title: The Armed Alternative
nodes.description: Material assistance can strengthen an armed opposition with a genuine local political base. A wider confrontation carries risks for both the Syrian population and American commitments.
requirements: A locally supported Kurdish armed movement
A regional crisis or weakened central control
Strategic confrontation with Damascus

nodes.title: A Northern Political Authority
nodes.description: A new political authority must emerge from territory it actually controls and from the wishes of its representatives.
requirements: A successful local uprising
Kurdish local authority controls the eligible region
Local consent to the proposed status

nodes.title: Desert Storm
nodes.description: Iraq's attack on Kuwait threatens the sovereignty of the Gulf's states and the order on which their security depends. We will seek authority to use American military power to reverse the conquest, while leaving the commitment of forces in the hands of Washington and its coalition partners.
requirements: An unresolved Iraqi attack on Kuwait, including occupation after capitulation
Independent of all Kurdish support focuses

nodes.title: Desert Shield
nodes.description: The forces needed to defend the Gulf must reach the region before they can influence events there. We will approach friendly governments about staging rights and prepare the supply arrangements on which any sustained American deployment will depend.
requirements: An unresolved Iraqi attack on Kuwait, including occupation after capitulation
Independent of all Kurdish support focuses

nodes.title: Coalition Mandate
nodes.description: A response to the conquest of Kuwait will carry greater weight if regional and international governments accept a common purpose. We will seek their cooperation and negotiate the commitments they are willing to make, knowing that political endorsement alone does not place their forces under American command.
requirements: An unresolved Iraqi attack on Kuwait, including occupation after capitulation
Independent of all Kurdish support focuses

nodes.title: Open Northern Channels
nodes.description: Iraq's northern parties possess their own ambitions, grievances and memories of outside intervention. Opening channels to them will clarify what they seek from Washington and what they can undertake themselves. Public encouragement must be weighed against the consequences for people who may act upon it.

nodes.title: A Limited War
nodes.description: Our mandate in the Gulf is strongest when its objectives remain clear. We will concentrate on Kuwait's restoration and organize a disciplined humanitarian effort, accepting that restraint leaves Washington with less influence over the struggle for power inside Iraq.

nodes.title: Arm the Front
nodes.description: Covert financial and military aid could give Kurdish forces leverage against Baghdad. Supplying an underground movement requires a cooperating government on Iraq's northern frontier. This would widen the campaign beyond Kuwait and expose Washington to a conflict that declarations and arms alone cannot resolve.

nodes.title: Northern Access
nodes.description: Relief and protection in northern Iraq depend on supply routes through neighboring states. We will negotiate access with governments whose own interests in the Kurdish question may differ sharply from ours. Their cooperation must be maintained rather than taken for granted.

nodes.title: Provide Comfort
nodes.description: Fighting and displacement in the north have left communities beyond the reach of dependable public services. An American relief effort can keep essential supplies moving and help damaged infrastructure recover, provided neighboring governments allow the necessary routes to remain open.

nodes.title: Northern Safe Haven
nodes.description: A protected relief area requires more than a declaration. We will support the logistics of an accessible northern refuge, while recognizing that the security of its inhabitants still depends on the forces present and the willingness of outside governments to remain involved.

nodes.title: Northern Air Shield
nodes.description: American and cooperating air forces can make attacks on the northern communities more difficult. We will prepare interception, air-superiority and liaison arrangements from consenting bases. The commitment must be sustained by actual aircraft and the governments willing to host them.

nodes.title: Regional Assembly
nodes.description: Local councils and party administrations must provide more than military leadership if the north is to recover. We will support representative institutions and a functioning regional budget, while allowing the Kurdish parties to negotiate their own relationship and priorities.

nodes.title: Baghdad Accord
nodes.description: An agreement with Baghdad could turn an uncertain refuge into recognized self-government within Iraq. We will seek terms that protect regional budgets and local security, and support reconstruction only once the governments concerned accept and uphold the settlement.

nodes.title: Guarantee Self-Rule
nodes.description: The regional administrations may be unable to secure dependable guarantees from Baghdad. An external American commitment would strengthen their defence, but would also leave Washington responsible for a costly undertaking that Iraq's government continues to contest.

nodes.title: Northern Recovery
nodes.description: Northern recovery needs roads, functioning administration and an economy able to support returning families. We will negotiate assistance with the local authorities and support practical reconstruction, whether their security rests on an accepted Iraqi settlement or a continuing external commitment.

iraq.name: IRAQ
iraq.actors: KDP / Barzani; PUK only after its formation
iraq.note: Early assistance precedes the Kuwait crisis. Iraqi defeat can accelerate an existing campaign; it does not create an automatic rebellion.
iraq.penalty: Limited commitments require an accepted transit route.

iran.name: IRAN
iran.note: The Shah is a US partner in the 1970 opening. A hostile regime or a deliberate diplomatic breach is required.
iran.penalty: A breach suspends cooperation with Tehran and damages relations.

turkey.name: TURKEY
turkey.actors: Local organisations appropriate to the campaign
turkey.note: Turkey is a NATO ally. Preserve the Alliance and Challenge an Ally are mutually exclusive policies.
turkey.penalty: Breach: -150 Political Power; -75 relations; -10% Foreign Influence for 180 days.

syria.name: SYRIA
syria.actors: Syrian Kurdish civic and political representatives
syria.note: A 1970 programme begins with local political networks. Armed escalation requires an actual local movement and crisis.
syria.penalty: No later organisations or automatic transfer of neighbouring Kurdish governments.

campaign_lifecycle.garrison: Sustained funded operations build stabilisation gains. Withdrawal ends direct troop effects, but accumulated gains decay slowly and can keep unrest contained for an extended period.
campaign_lifecycle.funding: Standing weekly commitments until changed or suspended, without automatic ninety-day expiry.
campaign_lifecycle.persistence: Separate country ledgers retain regional unrest, mobilisation and spending across policy changes. Containment and accepted autonomy do not delete the system.
campaign_lifecycle.presentation: One visible regional unrest bar, three defender responses and one uprising warning. Costs remain available in an expandable section.
campaign_lifecycle.stabilisation: Hidden balance reserve from sustained operations and investment. No instant loss on withdrawal; no permanent immunity.
campaign_lifecycle.warning: Mobilisation buildup and response warning remain separate from deployment duration.

sources.label: US aid to Iraqi Kurds, 1974 memorandum

guardrails: A victim government does not approve hostile covert pressure.
Transit hosts and existing Kurdish RP players approve their own agreements.
Four separate host campaigns; no existing KUR or PUK player is overwritten.
No automatic country release or land transfer.
Kuwait intervention remains independent of the Kurdish campaign.
Iraqi occupation after Kuwaiti capitulation remains a valid crisis.
Each active campaign consumes a policy slot and continuing funding.
Defenders receive regional indicators and warnings, not the sponsor’s classified budget or cache before exposure.
Regions outside Iraq are illustrative local communities, not validated releasable state borders.

evidence.balance: All new focus rewards, costs and contest rates are proposals. The simulation illustrates counterplay, not measured engine behaviour.
evidence.actual_existing_warning: Two Iraqi states at resistance >=80 for 30 qualifying days, followed by a 45-day warning; 15 days below eligibility resets the existing warning.
